pages.name: A steady 3 C each second
pages.text: An ampere is one coulomb passing a point each second. An example cable carries a steady 3 C every second, `q = 3t`, so the current is 3 A wherever P goes: the slope of the charge graph, `i = dq/dt`. On a straight line the tangent is the line itself. Drag P.

pages.name: The current at 4 s
pages.task: Now the charge passed is `q = 0.5t²` coulombs, an example rule, and P is at 4 s. The power rule gives `dq/dt = 0.5 × 2t = t`. What is the current at 4 s, the height of P's dot below?
pages.why: `dq/dt = t`, so at 4 s the current is 4 A, and P's dot sits at 4. The graph stands at `0.5 × 16 = 8` C, which is how much charge has passed, and the chord from the start gives `8 ÷ 4 = 2` A on average. Only the tangent's slope says how fast at that instant.

pages.name: A capacitor
pages.text: An example 0.01 F capacitor, its voltage on top. Its current, below, is its capacitance times the voltage's slope: `i = C dv/dt`. While the voltage climbs 5 V each second, that is `0.01 × 5 = 0.05` A, 50 mA. Once it holds at 20 V the slope is 0, so for an ideal capacitor the current is 0, however high it is held.

pages.name: Held at 50 V
pages.task: The same capacitor is charged at 5 V each second up to 50 V, then held there, steady. P is on the steady part. What current flows through it now?
pages.why: Held steady, the voltage graph is flat, so its slope is 0 and the current is `0.01 × 0 = 0`, however high it is held. `0.01 × 50 = 0.5` A uses the height, and 50 mA is the current while it climbed.

pages.name: Charging through a resistor
pages.text: A sketch: a capacitor charged from a steady supply through a resistor. What is left across the resistor sets the current, and that same current charges the capacitor. At first that is the whole supply, so the current is largest and the voltage climbs fastest; as less is left, the current falls away towards zero.

pages.name: The largest current
pages.task: On the same charging sketch, when is the current through the capacitor largest?
pages.why: The current follows how fast the voltage climbs, and the climb is steepest at the start, when the voltage is lowest. At the end the voltage is highest but has nearly levelled off, so almost no current flows. A steady current would make the voltage climb in a straight line.

pages.name: A coil
pages.text: A coil, an inductor, swaps the roles: the voltage across it is its inductance times how fast its current changes, `v = L di/dt`. In an example 0.5 H coil, while the current climbs 4 A each second the voltage is `0.5 × 4 = 2` V; holding steady, 0 V; falling 4 A each second, −2 V.

pages.name: Switched off fast
pages.task: The same coil carries 2 A, and a switch cuts it to 0 in 0.01 s, so the current falls at `−2 ÷ 0.01 = −200` A per s. What voltage is across the coil while it falls?
pages.why: While the current falls, `v = 0.5 × −200 = −100` V: a large voltage, the other way round, because the current changes so fast. `0.5 × 2 = 1` V uses how big the current is, and 0 V is what is left once the current has stopped.

pages.name: Velocity and acceleration
pages.text: Motion adds a second step. The slope of displacement `s`, how far along from the start, is the [[velocity]]; the slope of the velocity is the [[acceleration]], the [[second derivative]]. The speeding boat, `s = t²` metres, at 3 s is 9 m along, doing `2 × 3 = 6` m per s, and its acceleration is 2 at every moment.

pages.name: The trolley at the top
pages.task: An example trolley is shoved up a long ramp: `s = 8t − t²` metres up it after `t` seconds. Its velocity is `8 − 2t`, so at 4 s it is 16 m up and stopped for an instant. What is its acceleration then, in m per s each second?
pages.why: The velocity line falls 2 m per s every second, all the way, from going up to coming down, so the acceleration is −2, even at the top. After 4 s the velocity is below 0: a minus velocity means moving the minus way, here back down the ramp. A velocity of 0 does not mean an acceleration of 0, and 16 m is how far up it is.

pages.task: An example cable passes `q = 2t² + 3t` coulombs after `t` seconds. What is the current at 2 s?
pages.why: Term by term, `dq/dt = 4t + 3`, so at 2 s the current is `4 × 2 + 3 = 11` A. 14 is the charge passed by then, `8 + 6 = 14` C, and 19 comes from not lowering the power: `4 × 4 + 3 = 19`.

pages.name: A capacitor, mixed
pages.task: An example 0.01 F capacitor has its voltage raised by the rule `v = t²` volts after `t` seconds. What current flows at 3 s?
pages.why: The voltage's slope at 3 s is `2 × 3 = 6` V per s, so the current is `0.01 × 6 = 0.06` A, 60 mA. `0.01 × 9` uses the voltage's height, and 6 is the slope alone, in volts per second: times the capacitance, it gives amps.
